content: To develop the framework, evidence was collected from existing literature, consultations with national and regional staff, and interviews with tuberculosis (TB) survivors and key stakeholders. In 2020, a policy review was conducted to evaluate the adoption of World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations on TB and comorbidities within national TB strategic plans and guidelines. In 2021, a systematic review was commissioned to identify barriers and enablers of collaborative care for individuals with TB and comorbidities. Focus group discussions were held between June and August 2021 with representatives from 16 countries across all six WHO regions to identify key challenges and opportunities for scaling up collaborative action on TB and comorbidities. Participants included representatives from ministries of health, national TB programs, programs addressing comorbidities, health systems, and WHO country and regional offices. Additionally, interviews with individuals with lived experiences of TB and comorbidities were conducted in August and September 2021 to assess barriers and preferences for accessing people-centered healthcare. A summary of the barriers and enablers identified during the consultations, interviews, and literature review is provided in Annex 2. In October 2021, a stakeholder consultation involving a wide range of experts, including representatives from the Civil Society Task Force on TB and TB survivors, was held to gather input on the draft framework. The revised draft underwent peer review by an external group between December 2021 and January 2022. Experts involved in the framework's development completed a declaration of interests form in line with WHO processes (Annex 3). The framework will be translated and published electronically on the WHO Global TB Programme website. It will also be referenced in future clinical guideline updates and operational handbooks for TB and related comorbidities. To accelerate the implementation of actions on TB and comorbidities, WHO will collaborate with partners to disseminate the framework through regional and subregional meetings. Training modules will be developed to support the adoption of the framework alongside relevant guidelines. The framework is intended for use by individuals working in ministries of health, particularly those involved in national programs for TB, HIV, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), primary healthcare, tobacco cessation, undernutrition, substance use, and mental health. It is also targeted at policymakers, international technical and funding organizations, researchers, non-governmental and civil society organizations, primary care workers, specialist health practitioners, and community health workers in both public and private sectors. The framework outlines actions to support countries in introducing and scaling up collaborative efforts on TB and comorbidities. It is structured around six core principles and organized into sections A to E, which detail key actions for ensuring people-centered services. These sections are logically ordered to facilitate the stepwise implementation and scale-up of collaborative action on TB and comorbidities. The framework aims to support the implementation of WHO recommendations and guidelines on TB and comorbidities, as listed in Annex 1, and related updates available on the Global TB Programme Knowledge Sharing Platform. Health programs should aim to implement collaborative actions for all identified comorbidities across the continuum of care, including prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and post-TB care. A phased approach, starting with a few comorbidities based on local epidemiology and feasibility, will help achieve this goal. Services should be continuously evaluated and adapted as needed. The framework emphasizes strengthening governance and accountability for collaborative action, finding and treating TB among individuals with key health-related risk factors, and implementing people-centered care. It also highlights the importance of protecting human rights, promoting equity, engaging affected communities and civil society, and achieving universal health coverage. Collaborative actions should include preventing TB among individuals with identified risk factors, preventing comorbidities among people with TB, and addressing comorbidities in individuals with TB. The framework also provides case studies to illustrate successful collaborative actions, such as integrating TB, HIV, and substance use care in Moldova, addressing TB and mental health at the community level in Peru, and implementing collaborative TB and diabetes care in Mexico. These examples demonstrate the importance of political commitment, enabling legal frameworks, capacity building, and community engagement in achieving effective and sustainable outcomes.
